problem: Many imitation-learning visuomotor controllers, such as behaviour cloning with CNN regression, are not goal-directed by design, so they cannot be used for goal-directed navigation. Existing learned topological or planning methods need heavy RL training, perfect odometry, or human low-level control, or they lack real-world demonstrations. End-to-end regression controllers also suffer cascading rotational errors and are brittle to environment changes.
motivation: Imitation learning lets robots acquire complex sensorimotor skills from demonstrations instead of programming, and humans compose simple learned behaviours to reach complex goals. A modular way to chain reactive, non-goal-directed trajectory-following skills into a goal-directed system would make imitation learning usable for practical indoor navigation such as buildings and corridors. That system should also be interpretable and incrementally extendable.
key_idea: Represent the environment as a directed graph whose vertices are learned (trajectory-classifier, trajectory-imitation-controller) pairs and whose edges are intersection classifiers, then plan over it with Dijkstra and switch reactive controllers at recognised intersections until a goal image is recognised.
insight: Goal-directed navigation does not need metric localisation: minimal topological localisation (which trajectory am I on, am I at an intersection) is enough to sequence reactive imitation skills. Casting steering as detecting a 'direction-of-motion' bounding box (RetinaNet + PID) is more robust than regressing motor commands. On L1-L3 the regression controller starts slightly higher (99.8–99.9% PA, after several DAgger iterations) but degrades more after 4 weeks (up to 2.9 points on L1), while the detector degrades at most 0.9 points without any DAgger. The authors attribute this to DAgger over-fitting to the appearance at collection time. For the detector, offline test loss also correlated with real-world performance, which was not the case for the regression controller.
method: Regression trajectory controller: frozen ImageNet-pretrained CNN encoder (MobileNetV2) + trainable MLP [2048,1024,256,32,2] with ReLU, trained by ridge-regularised MSE behaviour cloning with Adam; uses DAgger and augmentation (input/output shifting, random lighting, regional dropout); output clipped to [-1.5,1.5] control-pad range.

Object-detection-based trajectory controller: COCO-pretrained RetinaNet fine-tuned (SGD with momentum) to detect a single-class 896×360 bounding box. The box is centred when driving straight and shifted horizontally toward the rotation direction; a PID controller with error e_t = x_t − x_c (box centre x minus image centre x) produces the steering command.

Trajectory classifier g: frozen MobileNetV2 + MLP [512,256,32,C] with softmax over the C trajectories, trained with cross-entropy; gives topological localisation and identifies the goal trajectory via argmax_i g(X*).

Intersection classifiers h and goal-reaching function r: a proprietary keypoint object-recognition engine (derived from Find-Object) using FAST corners and BRIEF descriptors; it memorises each intersection or goal from a few images, avoiding per-intersection labelled training.

TNG planning/execution: directed graph G=(V,E) with vertices = (controller, trajectory classifier) and edges = intersection classifiers. Dijkstra finds the shortest vertex path from the current to the goal trajectory. The corresponding controllers run and are switched at recognised intersections; the goal-trajectory controller then runs until r recognises the goal image.

setting.backbone: MobileNetV2 (ImageNet-pretrained, frozen) + trained MLP for regression controller/trajectory classifiers; RetinaNet (COCO-pretrained, fine-tuned) + PID for detection controller; FAST/BRIEF keypoint matcher for intersections/goal
setting.training_data: Teleoperated demonstrations in the target environments: each trajectory driven 3 times, recording front RGB images and motor commands. Plus several DAgger iterations (regression controller only) and data augmentation; a few images per intersection/goal for the keypoint recogniser. Exact dataset sizes are shown only in a figure.
setting.observation: monocular front-facing RGB camera (goal specified as an image)
setting.action_space: continuous steering/motor command clipped to the SentiBotics control-pad range [-1.5, 1.5]
setting.simulator: Gazebo (SentiBotics simulation modules) plus real world
setting.privileged: Environment-specific prior demonstrations of every trajectory (teach-and-repeat style pre-exploration) and a manually designed navigation graph; human interventions allowed during evaluation (measured by percentage autonomy)

numbers_note: All evaluations are on the authors' own real-robot/Gazebo environments with percentage autonomy (PA) as the metric; no standard benchmark and no external baselines. Table 2 also gives per-pair PA (range 92.1–99.1) and per-pair distances (8.5–96.1 m) for all 20 source→destination trajectory pairs; only the mean PA and total distance are recorded here, and both are printed as approximate. The TNG experiment does not state which trajectory controller type was used. Data-point counts are only shown in a figure (Fig. 'Number of data points used to achieve reported scores').
results: Both trajectory imitation controllers reach ≥97% percentage autonomy in real environments and 99.9–100% in simulation. The regression controller scores slightly higher right after DAgger training (99.8–99.9%) but loses 0.6–2.9 points after 4 weeks. The RetinaNet-based controller loses only 0.2–0.9 points and needs no DAgger. The full TNG system navigated between all 20 trajectory pairs in a real office during working hours, with mean percentage autonomy ≈96.3% (per-pair 92.1–99.1%) over ≈1.1 km; no external navigation baselines were compared.
limitations: Assumes the environment is covered by separable, intersecting trajectories: nearly parallel nearby trajectories are hard to discriminate, and paths are geometrically sub-optimal.

Requires significant human effort: teleoperated demonstrations per trajectory, DAgger for the regression controller, and manual design of the navigation graph. The system only works in pre-demonstrated environments (no generalisation to new environments).
Small-scale custom evaluation (a few trajectories, a single metric of percentage autonomy with human intervention) and no comparison to other navigation methods.
builds_on: End-to-end behaviour cloning for driving (Bojarski et al. 2016, PilotNet)
